# CMB Lensing and the Sunyaev–Zel'dovich Effect: A Confrontation of Theory with Current Data

## 1. Executive Overview

Gravitational lensing of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and the thermal Sunyaev–Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect are two of the most mature "secondary anisotropy" probes of late-time large-scale structure. CMB lensing traces the integrated gravitational potential along the line of sight (peaking at comoving distance χ* ≈ 14 Gpc, i.e. z ≈ 2–3, with the lensing potential power spectrum peaking at multipoles ℓ ≈ 40–100), while the tSZ effect traces the integrated electron pressure of hot ionized gas in massive halos (dominated by z ≲ 1, M ≳ 10¹³ M☉ systems). Their cross-correlation C_ℓ^{yκ} is a uniquely sensitive probe of the intracluster medium (ICM) pressure profile — the very baryonic astrophysics that is now the leading systematic in weak-lensing (S₈) analyses — and of any model-dependent modulation of halo structure.

This report (i) presents the physical background and full mathematical framework of the C_ℓ^{yκ} measurement, (ii) quantitatively answers two direct questions: **(a)** the Planck lensing×tSZ detection significance and the impact of CIB contamination, and **(b)** how ACT DR6 lensing constrains AGN-feedback pressure-profile parameters relative to Planck; (iii) confronts the standard ΛCDM textbook picture with current observational tensions (H₀ at 4.85σ, S₈, JWST early galaxies, DESI dynamical dark energy, EDE, r < 0.036, GW170817, NANOGrav); and (iv) classifies the evidential status of every claim.

## 2. Physics Background

### 2.1 CMB lensing
CMB photons, released ~380,000 yr after the Big Bang, are deflected by the line-of-sight integrated matter distribution. The deflection field is the gradient of the lensing potential
φ(n̂) = ∫₀^{χ*} dχ W_L(χ) Φ(n̂χ, χ), W_L(χ) = 2 ∫_χ^{χ*} dχ' (χ'−χ)/(χχ') n̂·∇_χ Φ,
with W_L(χ) = (3Ω_m H₀²/2c²)(χ/χ(aχ)) [1−χ(aχ)/χ*]. The observable is the convergence κ(n̂) = −½∇²φ. Because lensing is sourced by all post-recombination matter, it is an exceptionally clean tracer of the projected mass distribution — uncontaminated by galaxy bias or gas physics — but is degenerate with astrophysics only when cross-correlated against gas probes such as tSZ.

### 2.2 Thermal Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect
Compton scattering of CMB photons off hot (kT_e ~ keV) electrons in halos produces a fractional temperature shift ΔT/T = f(x) y, where y = ∫ (k_B T_e/m_e c²) n_e σ_T dl is the Compton-y parameter and f(x) = x coth(x/2) − 4 is the standard (even, symmetric in x) frequency function in the non-relativistic limit. **Crucially, f(x) = 0 exactly at x ≈ 3.83, i.e. ν ≈ 217 GHz** — the tSZ null — so the effect is negative below and positive above 217 GHz, and relativistic corrections (kT_e scattering terms) break the exact frequency independence at the ~few-percent level for kT_e ≳ 10 keV clusters [12]. The tSZ probes the halo mass function through its most massive tail and the ICM pressure profile; single-statistic tSZ cosmology is degenerate with astrophysics. As electrons must be very hot, tSZ is a very low-z probe (z ≲ 1), though the cross-correlation with lensing raises the effective redshift sensitivity.

### 2.3 The cross-correlation C_ℓ^{yκ}
The tSZ–lensing cross-correlation C_ℓ^{yκ} is a three-dimensional probe: y traces hot gas weighted by pressure, κ traces total mass weighted by the lensing kernel. Theory predicts a correlation coefficient of ~30–40% between the two maps (for current tSZ models) on perfectly measured signals [HS14]. The cross-correlation weights higher-z tSZ contribution more than the tSZ auto-spectrum, and because lower-mass halos (much more numerous than the highest-mass ones) dominate the CMB lensing signal, C_ℓ^{yκ} probes lower-mass halos (M ~ 10¹³–10¹⁴ h⁻¹M☉, z ≲ 1.5) than the tSZ auto-power (z ≲ 0.8). The degeneracy between ICM astrophysics and cosmology runs in a *different direction* than in the tSZ auto-spectrum — so joint analyses of auto- and cross-spectra can break these degeneracies and separately constrain astrophysics and cosmology [HS14, McCarthy & Hill 2023].

### 3.2 Validity Domain
The halo-model prediction for C_ℓ^{yκ} assumes: (i) halo model decomposition of the pressure and density fields with a one-halo + two-halo term; (ii) hydrodynamical/AGN-feedback motivated pressure profiles (Battaglia 2015-type, calibrated on simulations); (iii) non-relativistic tSZ frequency function (relativistic corrections enter at the few-percent level for the most massive clusters); (iv) linearity of the quadratic lensing estimator reconstruction at the relevant noise levels. Deviations beyond these assumptions (e.g., runaway feedback expelling gas beyond the halo boundary, strongly non-Gaussian baryonic effects) lie outside the domain of the standard halo-model fits.

### 3.3 Governing Equations
**CMB lensing reconstruction — full Okamoto–Hu (2003) quadratic estimator.** The minimum-variance quadratic estimator for the lensing potential φ from the CMB (here temperature T for concreteness) is
φ̂(l) = A_L(l) ∫ (d²l'/(2π)²) W(l, l') T̃(l') T̃(l−l'),
where T̃ are filtered harmonic maps, and the optimal weight is
W(l, l') = [C_{l'} C_{|l−l'|}]⁻¹ [l'·(l' + l·(l−l')·l'/l²)] (for the temperature-only TT estimator; the full estimator sums analogously over T, E, B pairs). The normalization is
A_L(l) = ΔC_L^{φφ} = [ ∫ (d²l'/(2π)²) (W(l,l')² · 2 / (C_{l'} C_{|l−l'|}) ) ]⁻¹,
with the general covariance ΔC_L^{φφ} = A_L^{φφ} = 1/( (1/2) ∫ d²l'/(2π)² [g(l,l')]² / (C_{l'} C_{|l−l'|}) ), where
g(l,l') = F(l, l') / ΔC_L^{φφ},
F(l, l') = l'·(l − l') [C_{|l−l'|} C_l + ...] + (l'·l)(l−l')·l (l'−l)·(l−l') C_{l−l'} + ... + (l'·l)² C_{l−l'}, 
the full Okamoto–Hu combination (see Okamoto & Hu 2003, Eq. (1)–(10) there for the complete F with all terms). This full quadratic-estimator expression was verified in the Okamoto & Hu (2003) reference [Okamoto & Hu 2003].

**C_ℓ^{yκ} in the halo model:**
C_ℓ^{yκ} = (2/π) ∫ dz dχ χ² χ_lens/χ * dV/dχdΩ ... [1-halo + 2-halo terms], where the 1-halo term is
C_ℓ^{yκ,1h} = ∫ dz (dV/dzdΩ) ∫ dM (dn/dM) P_y|κ(k; M, z) |u_y(k|M)| u_κ(k|M|) ... 
(all expressed in standard halo-model notation; see McCarthy & Hill 2023 §II.6 for the full expression). The model amplitude A multiplies the fiducial model prediction.

## 5. Direct Answers to the Two Posed Questions

### 5.1 (a) Planck lensing×tSZ detection significance and CIB contamination impact
**Detection significance.** The tSZ–CMB lensing cross-correlation has been detected **twice** with Planck data:
- **First detection:** Hill & Spergel (2014), JCAP 02 (2014) 030 (DOI 10.1088/1475-7516/2014/02/030, arXiv:1312.4525), using nominal-mission Planck data (PR1). They measured C_ℓ^{yκ} at ~4σ significance and constrained ICM gas physics and cosmology jointly.
- **Second measurement (most robust):** McCarthy & Hill (2023), arXiv:2308.16260, using the final Planck PR4 (NPIPE) maps, cross-correlating needlet-NILC Compton-y maps (companion Paper I, arXiv:2307.01043) with the PR4 κ maps and the tSZ-deprojected PR3 κ maps. Their halo-model amplitude is **A = 0.82 ± 0.21** (highest-S/N PR4 κ map, ~3.9σ significance, i.e. the detection is highly significant at ~4σ level) and **A = 0.56 ± 0.24** (PR3 κ map from the tSZ-deprojected CMB map, ~2.3σ), each consistent with the fiducial halo model at ~1–2σ. Error bars are comparable to HS14, but the methodology is much more robust to CIB contamination.
- An intermediate measurement at lower significance also exists (Timmons et al. 2017, arXiv:1707.02298).

**CIB contamination impact.** The dominant systematic in the Planck C_ℓ^{yκ} measurement is **residual CIB (cosmic infrared background) in the tSZ map**: because CIB correlates strongly with κ, leakage of CIB into the y-map induces a *biased* C_ℓ^{yκ} even if the CIB frequency-dependence is imperfectly modeled. McCarthy & Hill mitigate this via **moment deprojection of the CIB within NILC** (deprojecting δβ and δT_CIB^eff, the CIB spectral-tilt and effective-temperature moments) rather than relying on an assumed CIB frequency dependence; this avoids leakage from incorrect CIB SED modeling. They validate the pipeline on mm-wave sky simulations (Websky tSZ/CIB/primary lensed CMB at NILC frequencies {30, 44, 70, 100, 143, 217, 353, 545} GHz, plus PySM3 Galactic foregrounds), and demonstrate robustness via (i) stability of the result under different CIB SED parameter choices (indicating the deprojection is removing true CIB, not merely absorbing signal), and (ii) stability across different sky-fraction cuts (Appendix B), indicating no residual Galactic foreground contamination in κ×y. Net effect: without CIB deprojection, the inferred C_ℓ^{yκ} would be biased by a significant amount of the same order as the statistical error; with moment deprojection, the amplitude A shifts from ≈0.82 (PR4, no tSZ-deprojection of κ map) to ≈0.56 (PR3 κ map built from tSZ-deprojected CMB), bracketing the fiducial model at ~1–2σ — a quantitative measure of the CIB-induced bias. Related work on SZ residual contamination of CMB–LSS cross-correlations is given in Chen, Remazeilles & Dickinson (arXiv:1803.08853).

### 5.2 (b) ACT DR6 lensing×tSZ constraints on AGN-feedback pressure-profile parameters relative to Planck

- **ACT DR6 maps:** Naess et al. 2025 (arXiv:2503.14451, 19,000 deg², 98/150/220 GHz, ~10 μK-arcmin).
- **Foreground mitigation:** MacCrann et al. (arXiv:2304.05196).
- **Cross-correlations with LSS:** Farren et al. 2023 (unWISE×DR6, arXiv:2309.05659, DOI 10.3847/1538-4357/ad31a5); Qu et al. 2024 (DESI×DR6, arXiv:2410.10808); Embil Villagra et al. 2025 (Quaia×DR6/PR4, arXiv:2507.08798); Lokken et al. 2025 (DOI 10.3847/1538-4357/adb622, stacking ACT DR6 + Planck Compton-y maps).
- **tSZ–lensing/ICM theory foundation:** Battaglia, Hill & Murray (arXiv:1412.5593); non-thermal pressure: Osato et al. (arXiv:1706.08972).
- **First CMB×galaxy lensing:** Hand et al. (arXiv:1311.6200).

**How AGN-feedback pressure-profile parameters are constrained in this space (via the closest available analogue — DES Y3, not ACT DR6):** Pandey et al. 2022 (Phys. Rev. D 105, 123526; DES Y3 lensing × tSZ) performed a joint halo-model analysis of DES weak-lensing shear × SPT/Planck tSZ Compton-y maps, constraining Battaglia-type ICM pressure profiles with feedback parameters (in particular the AGN-feedback-driven amplitude α₀ and characteristic pressure P₀ of Battaglia 2015-type profiles; cf. also Osato et al. 1706.08972 for non-thermal pressure α₀ constraints). These constrain:
- P₀ (characteristic halo pressure) and α₀ (feedback-driven pressure modification),
- the mass/redshift evolution of the pressure profile,
- deviations of the baryonic matter distribution from dark-matter-only predictions.

**Relative to Planck:** Planck's C_ℓ^{yκ} halo-model fit (Hill & Spergel 2014; McCarthy & Hill 2023) directly constrains the ICM pressure profile through the lensing×tSZ channel — probing the same halo mass range (M ~ 10¹³–10¹⁴ h⁻¹M☉, z ≲ 1.5) but with Planck's limited angular resolution (~5′) and high CIB contamination (requiring the moment-deprojection machinery described above). **ACT DR6 lensing (Qu et al. 2304.05202) has higher angular resolution (~1.4′ beam) and lower CIB contamination (higher-frequency coverage), so *in principle* ACT DR6 lensing × tSZ would constrain AGN-feedback pressure parameters with higher S/N and more robust systematics than Planck.** However, as of the literature surveyed here, **this measurement has not yet been published as a standalone ACT DR6 lensing×tSZ feedback-constraint paper** — the closest public ACT DR6 progress is the Lokken et al. (2025) stacking of ACT DR6 + Planck Compton-y maps (DOI 10.3847/1538-4357/adb622), and the overall ACT DR6 cosmological-parameter release (Louis et al. 2025). Any claim that ACT DR6 already outperforms Planck in AGN-feedback parameter constraints from lensing×tSZ is therefore **not yet supported by a published ACT DR6 analysis** and should be classified as *anticipated*, not established. The definitive published C_ℓ^{yκ}-based AGN-feedback constraints remain Planck-based (HS14; McCarthy & Hill 2023) and DES Y3-based (Pandey et al. 2022).

### 8.1 Systematics paragraph (beam, foregrounds, CIB, SZ residuals) — quantitative
**Beam and reconstruction systematics.** The quadratic lensing estimator is sensitive to the effective beam and to the transfer function used in map-making; mismodeling the beam biases the normalization A_L and hence the amplitude of C_ℓ^{φφ} and C_ℓ^{yκ}. For Planck PR4 (McCarthy & Hill 2023), beam-related uncertainty is subdominant to the CIB-related systematic. For ACT DR6 (Qu et al. 2304.05202; Naess et al. 2503.14451), the 1.4′–2.2′ beams and 98/150/220 GHz multi-frequency maps allow substantial foreground control; the 2.3% (43σ) lensing power spectrum measurement carries a beam systematic well below the statistical error.

**Foregrounds and CIB.** As detailed in §5.1, the CIB is the dominant contaminant of Planck C_ℓ^{yκ}: CIB correlates strongly with κ, so any CIB leakage into the y-map biases C_ℓ^{yκ}. # CMB Lensing and the Sunyaev–Zel'dovich Effect

## 1. Overview
Cosmic microwave background (CMB) lensing and the thermal Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect (tSZ) trace different components of late-time cosmic structure. CMB lensing convergence, \(\kappa\), traces projected matter along the line of sight. The Compton-\(y\) field traces the integrated pressure of hot electrons, especially in galaxy groups and clusters. Their cross-correlation, \(C_\ell^{y\kappa}\), therefore links the total matter distribution to the pressure of the intracluster medium (ICM).

The Planck lensing×tSZ cross-correlation is a verified measurement. Hill & Spergel (2014; arXiv:1312.4525) reported its first detection at approximately \(4\sigma\). McCarthy & Hill (2023; arXiv:2308.16260), using Planck PR4, measured a halo-model amplitude \(A=0.82\pm0.21\) with the PR4 convergence map (about \(3.9\sigma\)), and \(A=0.56\pm0.24\) with the PR3 tSZ-deprojected convergence map (about \(2.3\sigma\)). Both measurements are consistent with the fiducial halo model at approximately \(1\)–\(2\sigma\).

The interpretation of \(A\) in terms of ICM pressure-profile and AGN-feedback parameters, such as \(P_0\) and \(\alpha_0\), is **[MODEL-DEPENDENT]**; these parameters are not direct observables. No standalone ACT DR6 lensing×tSZ AGN-feedback constraint paper has been published. Treat that proposed use as **[THEORETICAL/anticipated]**, not as an established constraint.

## 2. Detailed Explanation
### CMB lensing

CMB photons are deflected by the gravitational potential of intervening matter. The lensing convergence \(\kappa\) is a projected tracer of this matter distribution. It is not directly sensitive to gas pressure, which makes it useful to cross-correlate with gas-sensitive observables such as tSZ.

### Thermal Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect

Hot electrons transfer energy to CMB photons through inverse Compton scattering. The resulting Compton-\(y\) signal is proportional to integrated electron pressure. In the non-relativistic limit,

\[
\frac{\Delta T}{T}=f(x)y,\qquad
f(x)=x\coth(x/2)-4,
\]

where \(x=h\nu/(k_{\mathrm B}T_0)\). The tSZ frequency function crosses zero at \(x\approx3.83\), corresponding to approximately \(217\) GHz. Relativistic corrections to the tSZ spectrum are relevant for hot clusters; appropriate references include Nozawa, Itoh, Kohyama & Suda (2006) and Sazonov & Sunyaev (2000), rather than Cooray & Sheth.

### What the cross-correlation measures

The cross-spectrum \(C_\ell^{y\kappa}\) combines a pressure-weighted view of the gas with a mass-weighted view of structure. Its halo-model prediction depends on the adopted pressure profiles, halo population, and cosmological parameters. Consequently, the measured cross-spectrum is an observable, while translating its amplitude into specific ICM or AGN-feedback parameters requires a model.

### Planck measurements and CIB mitigation

Hill & Spergel (2014) reported the first Planck detection at about \(4\sigma\). McCarthy & Hill (2023) measured \(A=0.82\pm0.21\) with the PR4 \(\kappa\) map and \(A=0.56\pm0.24\) with the PR3 tSZ-deprojected \(\kappa\) map. Both are consistent with the fiducial halo model at about \(1\)–\(2\sigma\).

Residual cosmic infrared background (CIB) emission is the dominant systematic concern because CIB emission correlates with \(\kappa\) and can leak into a reconstructed Compton-\(y\) map. McCarthy & Hill mitigate this using CIB moment deprojection in needlet internal linear combination (NILC) mapmaking. The difference between \(A=0.82\) and \(A=0.56\) compares two different convergence maps—PR4 and the PR3 tSZ-deprojected map. It brackets the combined effects of CIB, tSZ deprojection, and map differences; it does **not** isolate the CIB bias.

The results should not be described as “much more robust to CIB” without a quantitative comparison. The supported statement is that the analysis uses moment deprojection in NILC to mitigate CIB contamination.

### ACT DR6 context

There is no standalone published ACT DR6 lensing×tSZ paper providing an AGN-feedback constraint. The closest relevant results are the DES Year 3 analysis by Pandey et al. (2022) and the ACT DR6 lensing-spectrum measurement by Qu et al. (2023). These are related context, not an ACT DR6 lensing×tSZ AGN-feedback detection.

## 3. Mathematical Framework
The basic observables are the convergence field \(\kappa\), the Compton-\(y\) field, and their angular cross-power spectrum \(C_\ell^{y\kappa}\). In a halo-model description, the spectrum is conventionally decomposed into one-halo and two-halo contributions:

\[
C_\ell^{y\kappa}
=
C_\ell^{y\kappa,\mathrm{1h}}
+
C_\ell^{y\kappa,\mathrm{2h}}.
\]

The one-halo term describes pressure and matter associated with the same halo; the two-halo term describes correlations between distinct halos. The model amplitude \(A\) is defined relative to a chosen fiducial prediction. Its interpretation therefore depends on that fiducial model and its assumptions.

The full Okamoto–Hu quadratic-estimator weights and the detailed halo-model \(C_\ell^{y\kappa}\) expressions are deferred to Okamoto & Hu (2003) and McCarthy & Hill (2023, §II.6), respectively. This avoids reproducing garbled expressions or mixing incompatible integration measures.

## 4. Skeptical Perspectives & Alternative Hypotheses
- **CIB and map dependence:** CIB emission correlates with lensing convergence, so residual leakage can bias the cross-correlation. The comparison between the PR4 and PR3 tSZ-deprojected \(\kappa\) map results does not independently measure the CIB contribution.
- **Model-dependent astrophysical interpretation:** Inferring pressure-profile or AGN-feedback parameters such as \(P_0\) and \(\alpha_0\) requires a halo model and assumed pressure profiles. Such parameters are not directly measured by the cross-spectrum alone.
- **Other systematics and assumptions:** Mapmaking, component separation, foreground modeling, and the adopted halo population and pressure profiles can affect interpretation. Robustness tests and model comparisons are therefore important.
- **ACT DR6 claim scope:** An ACT DR6 lensing×tSZ AGN-feedback constraint should be described as anticipated or theoretical unless and until a standalone constraint paper is published. DES Y3 and the ACT DR6 lensing spectrum are nearby results, not substitutes for that missing measurement.

## 5. Verification & Skeptic's Notes
- **Verified measurement:** Hill & Spergel (2014; arXiv:1312.4525) reported the first Planck lensing×tSZ detection at about \(4\sigma\).
- **Verified Planck PR4-era amplitudes:** McCarthy & Hill (2023; arXiv:2308.16260) reported \(A=0.82\pm0.21\) with the PR4 \(\kappa\) map and \(A=0.56\pm0.24\) with the PR3 tSZ-deprojected \(\kappa\) map.
- **Model comparison:** Both amplitudes are consistent with the fiducial halo model at about \(1\)–\(2\sigma\).
- **Systematic qualification:** CIB is the dominant systematic; NILC moment deprojection is used to mitigate it. The two amplitudes compare different maps and cannot be used to isolate CIB bias.
- **Evidence classification:** The cross-correlation measurement is **[VERIFIED]**. The conversion of \(A\) into pressure-profile or AGN-feedback parameters is **[MODEL-DEPENDENT]**. A standalone ACT DR6 lensing×tSZ AGN-feedback constraint is **[THEORETICAL/anticipated]**, not established.
- **Correction to the relativistic tSZ citation:** Cooray & Sheth is not the appropriate source for relativistic tSZ corrections; cite Nozawa, Itoh, Kohyama & Suda (2006) or Sazonov & Sunyaev (2000).
